Trying to Conceive

Treatment approaches for vaginismus

Updated: October 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Vaginismus is an involuntary tightening of the muscles around the vaginal entrance. It can make vaginal penetration painful, difficult or sometimes impossible, including during intercourse or when trying to insert a finger. The response is automatic: it does not mean that someone is deliberately resisting, rejecting their partner or failing to cooperate. Treatment aims to help the person feel safer, understand the response and gradually gain more comfortable control.

Understanding the involuntary response

A helpful comparison is the way the eyelids close protectively when something suddenly approaches the eye. With vaginismus, an anticipated or attempted penetration can similarly be followed by muscle tightening before the person consciously chooses any response. Wanting intimacy does not necessarily switch that reaction off.

Fear of pain and the memory of an uncomfortable experience can contribute to a cycle: anticipated penetration brings anxiety, the muscles tighten, and a painful attempt reinforces the expectation that another attempt will hurt. Understanding that cycle can help explain why pressure, rushing or repeatedly trying to force penetration is unhelpful.

The symptoms are physical even when fear and learned responses are part of the picture. Assessment should also consider other sources of pain, such as dryness, irritation or infection. It is not appropriate to assume that every person with these symptoms has an exclusively psychological problem.

When the difficulty continues, it can affect confidence and create strain between partners. Those effects deserve attention, but relationship breakdown is not inevitable. People can also benefit from treatment after living with symptoms for a long time; a delayed diagnosis is not a reason to give up.

1. Psychological and psychosexual therapy

Talking therapy is one treatment approach. A therapist can help explore fears about penetration, expectations about sex and the effect of previous painful experiences. The purpose is not simply to insist on positive thinking. It is to understand what happens for the individual and work on responses that make intimacy feel threatening or difficult.

Sessions may involve the person alone or, if they wish, their partner. When both attend, the therapist may help them talk about misunderstandings, disappointment or pressure without treating either person as an opponent. The quality of communication outside sexual activity can influence how supported someone feels during treatment.

A treatment plan can combine counselling with physical approaches. Psychological support does not mean the muscle response is imaginary, and pelvic floor treatment does not mean that emotional experiences must be ignored. These parts of care can support one another.

A clinician can explain referral options and help identify a therapist with experience in sexual pain. You may request a clinician you feel comfortable with, including a female clinician, but effective care is not determined solely by the therapist’s gender.

Learning about the body and sexual expectations

Learning the location and function of the genital structures and pelvic floor muscles can make an unfamiliar or frightening response easier to understand. A therapist can explain what happens during arousal and why muscle tension can interfere with comfortable penetration.

Reliable educational material can also challenge the idea that intercourse must happen immediately, or that a first sexual experience has to follow a particular timetable. There is no obligation to achieve penetration on a wedding night, over a fixed number of nights or by a deadline set by somebody else.

Allowing time for communication, affection and comfortable touch can help remove performance pressure. Intimacy involves skills and understanding as well as desire; needing guidance is not a personal inadequacy.

Move at a pace that both people agree to, with the person experiencing symptoms controlling what happens to their body. Preparation and patience are useful, but they cannot guarantee that vaginismus will never occur. Nor is marrying at an older age an established explanation that should be used to blame someone for symptoms.

Cognitive behavioural therapy and relaxation

Cognitive behavioural therapy, or CBT, examines the relationship between thoughts, feelings and actions. In this context, work may include identifying frightening expectations about penetration, considering how those expectations developed and practising different responses with support.

This is more specific than being told to stop worrying. A therapist can help make the steps manageable and address anxiety or low mood that has developed alongside the sexual difficulty. The approach should be adapted to the person rather than assuming everyone has the same fear or history.

Breathing and relaxation techniques may be included to help someone notice and release tension. They are skills to learn, not a demand to become perfectly relaxed on command. If an exercise increases distress, that is useful information for the therapist and a reason to adjust the plan.

Hypnosis is sometimes proposed as an additional approach. It should not be presented as a necessary treatment or an established cure for everyone. Ask about the practitioner’s qualifications, the evidence for the proposed intervention and how it fits with the rest of your care.

Privacy and pressure from other people

Questions from relatives or friends about a couple’s sex life can create additional stress. The person receiving treatment decides what to share. It is reasonable to set a boundary, give a brief answer or say that the matter is private.

If you want to acknowledge that you are getting help, a simple explanation that treatment is underway can be enough. You do not have to provide intimate details or promise that the problem will be solved within a few weeks or months.

Supportive people can be helpful when their involvement is wanted. The goal is to reduce unwanted pressure, not to require every patient to keep treatment secret or exclude someone they trust.

2. Physical treatment and pelvic floor physiotherapy

A pelvic health physiotherapist with experience in vaginismus can help assess how the muscles tighten, release and coordinate. Ask the clinician arranging your care about an appropriate referral. This is different from assuming that all difficulty with penetration is caused by muscle weakness.

Treatment may include learning to recognize tension, practising comfortable breathing and relaxing the muscles around the pelvic openings. A therapist can help distinguish a gentle release from straining or pushing. The aim is more comfortable function and control, not the strongest possible squeeze.

An overactive pelvic floor may already struggle to return to a relaxed resting state. Adding repeated strengthening exercises without enough relaxation can make that problem worse. If muscles are both tight and weak, the therapist may address the tension before deciding whether strengthening is useful.

The assessment and exercises should be explained before they begin. You can discuss any concerns about touch or examination and ask to pause or stop. Treatment should proceed with your agreement and should not rely on enduring increasing pain.

What Kegel exercises involve: and why the plan must be individual

Kegel exercises usually involve contracting and releasing the pelvic floor muscles, which contribute to bladder and bowel control and support pelvic organs. Learning to recognize these muscles can be useful, but a vaginismus treatment plan should pay particular attention to the ability to let them relax.

If a clinician recommends a contraction-and-release exercise, ask them to check your technique. They can explain how to avoid substituting a strong squeeze of the buttocks or thighs and how to breathe normally. The release matters as much as the contraction.

Do not repeatedly stop and start urinating as an exercise. A description of the muscles used to interrupt urine flow is not an instruction to practise that action whenever you use the toilet.

There is no universal number of repetitions or hold duration suitable for everyone with vaginismus. Fixed routines can be inappropriate for an already overactive pelvic floor. Your therapist should decide whether you need strengthening, relaxation, coordination work or a combination.

Once a suitable exercise has been demonstrated, ask when to practise, what it should feel like and which symptoms mean you should stop. More repetitions are not automatically better. Pain or increased tension is a reason to review the exercise rather than intensify it.

Gradual practice with vaginal trainers or dilators

Some treatment programmes use vaginal trainers, also called dilators. These are purpose-made devices available in different sizes. Guided practice can help a person become more familiar with the sensation of something approaching or entering the vagina while retaining control of the pace.

The aim is not to force the vagina open or prove that it can accept the largest size. A therapist should explain the starting point, positioning, suitable lubrication, cleaning and how to recognize when an exercise is becoming uncomfortable.

Progression is gradual and individual. Moving to another size is not a competition, and there is no requirement to copy a sequence of finger insertion or a fixed stretching session from a general article. The right starting point may involve learning relaxation before any insertion is attempted.

If the therapist recommends home practice, agree on the session length and frequency and how to report difficulties. Stop or pause when pain or distress increases; forcing through it can reinforce the painful experience that treatment is trying to address.

A partner may help only if the person practising wants that involvement and remains in control. The partner’s role is support, not pushing the device further or deciding when it is time to progress. Individual practice is also an option.

Returning to sexual activity gradually

Treatment exercises and sexual activity do not have to become a test of whether the person is improving quickly enough. Talk with the therapist about how the skills being learned can be used in situations that matter to you.

Rushing into penetration before you feel ready can lead to another painful experience and renew the fear of the next attempt. A patient, supportive partner can help by respecting limits and accepting that affection does not have to lead to intercourse.

Agree on how to communicate discomfort and when to stop. There should be no penalty, argument or sense of failure if an activity needs to end. Comfortable closeness can remain part of a relationship while treatment continues.

3. Medicines and numbing treatments

Vaginismus is not usually approached as a problem that one medicine can solve. A clinician may nevertheless recommend medication for an associated condition, so a blanket statement that medicine is never needed would be misleading.

Sedatives or sleeping medicines should not be used on your own to make painful or unwanted penetration possible. If a medicine is proposed, ask what condition or symptom it is intended to treat, what the risks are and how it fits with the wider plan.

A numbing cream can reduce sensation without addressing the muscle response, fear or another cause of pain. Do not use one simply to push through discomfort. At the same time, some prescribed topical treatments have a role in other diagnosed vulval pain conditions; their suitability needs an individual assessment.

Guidance for partners

Recognize the difference between an involuntary muscle response and a deliberate decision to reject intimacy. Someone can care deeply about a partner, want sexual closeness and still experience tightening or pain. Accusations of being uncooperative make it harder to discuss what is happening.

Listen to how the experience feels and ask what support is wanted. That might involve attending a therapy session, helping arrange appointments or simply removing expectations about intercourse. Do not assume that participating in treatment gives a partner control over examinations or exercises.

If the problem has affected communication or confidence in the relationship, those issues can be addressed too. They are not proof that the relationship is beyond repair. Avoid turning every affectionate moment into an attempt to check whether penetration is now possible.

Myths can delay helpful care. Involuntary tightening is not evidence of a curse or a personal defect. Surgery on the hymen is not a general treatment for vaginismus; an actual anatomical condition would require a separate diagnosis. Similarly, lubricant may help friction but does not necessarily resolve the underlying difficulty by itself.

Seeking help and looking ahead

Embarrassment can make it difficult to arrange an appointment, particularly if you expect to be judged. Vaginismus is not your fault, and it is reasonable to seek a clinician who takes your symptoms seriously and explains the options respectfully.

An initial visit can begin with a conversation about when symptoms started, what attempts feel painful and what you would like treatment to help you do. Tell the clinician about concerns before any examination. You do not have to force painful penetration to demonstrate that the problem exists.

Treatment can help, including when symptoms have been present for a long time. However, a single success percentage or a guaranteed recovery date cannot predict your own course. Your clinician should explain what improvement may look like for your circumstances rather than promise a uniform result.

Review progress with the treating team. Less fear, better understanding of the muscle response and more comfortable control can be useful changes. If the plan is not helping, ask whether the diagnosis, exercises or support should be reconsidered rather than blaming yourself for not improving fast enough.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NHS guidance describes vaginismus as an automatic tightening response and recommends assessment for other causes of pain. Treatment can address feelings about penetration alongside gradual, therapist-guided physical practice.

Pelvic health guidance distinguishes muscle strength from the ability to relax. An overactive pelvic floor needs an individualized approach; simply increasing the number of contractions is not an appropriate universal treatment.

How BeMama can help

BeMama’s reproductive-health guides can help you understand terminology and prepare questions for a clinical appointment. They cannot diagnose vaginismus, assess pelvic floor function or replace individualized treatment from a qualified professional.

When to seek help

Seek a GP, gynecology, sexual-health or pelvic-health assessment if penetration is painful or difficult. Tell the clinician about other symptoms and previous experiences. Do not force an examination or exercise through increasing pain; ask for the plan to be adjusted.

Evidence notes updated: October 5, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Vaginismus involves an involuntary response; it is not deliberate resistance.
  • Psychosexual support, pelvic floor treatment and gradual guided practice can be combined.
  • Muscle relaxation needs attention; an automatic prescription for more Kegels is inappropriate.
  • Partner involvement is optional and should preserve the person’s control.
  • Treatment should address individual goals without guaranteed cure rates or deadlines.

Frequently asked questions

Does needing psychological support mean the pain is imaginary?

No. Fear, physical pain and involuntary muscle tightening can interact. Assessment should also consider other treatable causes of pain.

Should everyone follow the same Kegel routine?

No. A pelvic health professional should assess muscle tension and relaxation before deciding on an exercise programme.

Are dilators compulsory?

No. They are one possible part of treatment. Discuss their purpose, alternatives and suitability with the therapist.

Must my partner take part?

No. You can receive individual care and choose whether, when and how a partner becomes involved.

Is there a guaranteed time to recovery?

No. A useful plan has review points and can be adjusted, rather than promising the same result by the same date for everyone.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
